sentences.text: This dinosaur was a relatively small sauropod with a femur measuring 0.75 meters, reaching lengths of 7 to 9 meters and weighing between 1.8 and 3.5 metric tons.
It is unique among sauropods for having a sacrum composed of seven vertebrae.
The animal is believed to have had armor-like osteoderms on its body.
The scapula of Neuquensaurus resembles those of Saltasaurus, Opisthocoelicaudia, Lirainosaurus, and Alamosaurus.
In this species, the scapula is fused with the coracoid, a trait also seen in Opisthocoelicaudia.
Fossils of Neuquensaurus were found in the Anacleto Formation near the Neuquén River in Argentina.
Richard Lydekker originally named the species Titanosaurus australis in 1893 based on tail vertebrae and limb bones.
Jaime Eduardo Powell validly established the genus Neuquensaurus in 1992, transferring the type species to Neuquensaurus australis.
A 2008 study reconstructed the hind limb muscles of Neuquensaurus.
Neuquensaurus is classified as a derived saltasaurine, closely related to Saltasaurus, Rocasaurus, and Bonatitan.
John Stanton McIntosh assigned the species to the genus Saltasaurus in 1990, arguing the differences were not taxonomically significant enough for a separate genus.
Powell considered the species N. robustus to be non-diagnostic and classified it as a nomen dubium.
Neuquensaurus lived in Argentina during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 83 to 74.5 million years ago.
Other estimates suggest the animal lived from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 85.7 and 66 million years ago.
Analysis of vertebral centra suggests two distinct morphotypes in Neuquensaurus, potentially supporting the hypothesis that two different species existed.
